To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the intertidal cockles Austrovenus are protected from the detrimental trematode parasite Curtuteria by the anemone Anthopluera that uses their shells as substrate, and that the relationship between anemone and cockle densities explains 30% of spatial variation in the parasite loads of cockles.

(1) the mud flat anenome Anthopleura auroeradiata provides protection to cockles against parasitic infections and (2) the cockle Austroavenus stutchbury is host to the trematode Curtutaria australis that infects through the filtration current.

(i) the mud flat anenome Anthopleura aureo-radiata uses the shells of the cockle Austro-venus stutch-buryi as substrate for attachment; (ii) the anemones depress the rate of parasitic infection in cockles; and (iii) the relationship between anemones and cockles is a mutualistic association in which the former obtain substrate for attachment whereas cockles are provided with protection against parasitic infection.

a mutualistic relationship between two marine invertebrates, the mudflat anemone, Anthopleura aureo-radiata, and the cockle, Austrovenus.
